items.title: Memoir of a Murderer
items.reason: In the 118-minute theatrical film, former serial killer Kim Byeong-soo has dementia and fears that he may be responsible for new murders, while a suspicious collision with a bloodstained car points him toward policeman Tae-joo, who begins dating his daughter. The evidence and his understanding change at several points: a blood sample and number plate implicate Tae-joo, an altered memoir and swapped evidence undermine Byeong-soo's account, a forgotten week and a supposedly safe relative expose serious gaps in his memory, and a dropped recorder later preserves a confession that his mind could not. The recovered truth about his own earlier crimes and the final confrontation further reframe his apparent protectiveness. Thus real clues and answers recur across the beginning, middle and final act, although the story repeatedly pauses for dementia and family tragedy, and uncertainty itself sometimes substitutes for a new verified answer. The Reel Bits praises the unreliable-narrator tension and photography but questions the logic of some twists; AsianMovieWeb praises the performance and suspense while finding the subplots unfocused and some revelations predictable. The separate director's cut adds roughly ten minutes and materially changes the ending, so its more radical final ambiguity must not be assumed to describe the standard theatrical cut. This is a serial-killer psychological puzzle and pursuit, not a broad institutional conspiracy or a nonstop police procedural.

items.title: Mirage
items.reason: In Oriol Paulo's 128-minute Spanish thriller, Vera's warning to a boy through a television during a repeated electrical storm saves his life in 1989 but rewrites her 2014 life so that her daughter has never existed. Her attempt to recover the child develops alongside an actual cold murder inquiry: she seeks police help, provides a testable lead to a body hidden beneath a slaughterhouse, and the discovered remains expose a concealed affair and falsified disappearance. The inquiry into the rescued boy's later life then yields another consequential identity revelation about the inspector assisting her, explaining why her relationships and family history changed; a final intervention reshapes the timeline once more. These are distributed discoveries in the opening, middle and late film rather than a single last-minute twist, but the investigation competes with extensive maternal distress, romance and alternate-life melodrama, so mystery and revelation cadence should not be conflated with nonstop detective work. The Hollywood Reporter review excerpt collected by Rotten Tomatoes praises the intricate construction while finding limited depth, and other critics there question the length and whether the emotional story overwhelms the thriller. The camera/television mechanism enables the time anomaly, but is not a malicious technological antagonist; the period scenes do not make the overall film's visual craft retro or cheap.
